title: Title and occasion: 'London, 1802'
short: Titled 'London, 1802' in 1807; written in September 1802, just after Wordsworth's return from France during the Peace of Amiens.
body: The archive titles the sonnet by its first line; in Poems, in Two Volumes (1807) it is headed 'London, 1802' and stands among the 'Sonnets Dedicated to Liberty'. In August 1802, during the brief Peace of Amiens, Wordsworth and Dorothy crossed to Calais to see Annette Vallon and his daughter Caroline before his marriage to Mary Hutchinson. His later note on the companion sonnet 'Written in London, September, 1802' says it was composed 'immediately after my return from France to London', and that he was struck by the vanity and parade of England, especially its great towns, against the quiet and desolation of France. That mood of indictment governs this poem too: Milton is summoned as a remedy for national corruption, not only as a literary ancestor.

title: Milton and Wordsworth's turn to the sonnet
short: Wordsworth began writing sonnets in May 1802 after Dorothy read Milton's sonnets to him; this poem pays that debt openly.
body: Dorothy Wordsworth's Grasmere Journal for 21 May 1802 records that William wrote two sonnets on Buonaparte after she had read Milton's sonnets to him. In the 1838 advertisement to his collected sonnets Wordsworth said that admiration for some of Milton's sonnets first tempted him to write in that form. The political sonnets of 1802-3 take from Milton not only the Italian structure but the public, admonitory voice of poems such as 'On the Late Massacre in Piedmont' and the sonnets to Cromwell and Fairfax. John Bard McNulty traced these debts in detail; more recently P. J. Connell has read the sequence as Wordsworth's attempt to ground British liberty in the seventeenth-century revolution while his own politics were moving toward Burke.

title: fen / Of stagnant waters
short: England is a marsh of standing water: inert, unwholesome, cut off from any living current.
body: A fen is low, waterlogged ground; the stress here falls on 'stagnant', water that no longer flows and so breeds corruption. The run-on from 'fen' into 'Of stagnant waters' holds the reader in suspension before the image completes. Readers may compare Milton's own figure in Areopagitica, where truth is a 'streaming fountain' whose waters, if they stop moving, 'sick'n into a muddy pool of conformity and tradition'. No edition consulted here claims a deliberate echo, but the parallel suits a poem that invokes Milton as the voice of free, moving thought against national torpor. The image also anticipates the sestet's contrasting water, the sea of Milton's voice (l. 10).

title: altar, sword and pen, / Fireside
short: Metonymies for the Church, the armed services, literature and learning, and domestic life: every estate of the nation is indicted.
body: Each noun stands for an institution: 'altar' the established Church and its clergy, 'sword' the army and navy, 'pen' writers, scholars and lawyers, and 'Fireside' the private household. The list moves from public to private, so that no sphere escapes the charge. The catalogue is compressed in Milton's manner, and it pointedly includes the 'pen', Wordsworth's own trade; the poet is not exempt from 'We are selfish men' (l. 6). The asyndeton (no linking 'and' before 'Fireside') and the line break give the list the air of an accusation being read out.

title: hall and bower
short: An old doublet for the great house: the hall as public, masculine space, the bower as the inner, private chamber.
body: 'Hall' is the main public room of a lord's dwelling; 'bower' in its older sense is an inner chamber, especially a lady's private apartment, rather than a garden arbour. The pairing is archaic and ballad-like, and it gives the 'heroic wealth' of England an ancient, almost Anglo-Saxon pedigree, matching 'ancient English dower' in the next line. Wordsworth means the inherited moral riches of the great houses and the families who lived in them, not their material wealth, which in 1802 he thought all too abundant.

title: dower
short: An endowment or birthright: the 'inward happiness' that English institutions once inherited and have now forfeited.
body: A dower is strictly a widow's portion of her husband's estate, and by extension any dowry, gift or natural endowment. Wordsworth uses the legal sense figuratively: inward happiness was the inheritance settled on England, and it has been 'forfeited', another legal term for property lost through misconduct. The language of estates and title-deeds sharpens the paradox of a country rich in money and bankrupt in spirit. 'Inward happiness' is held over to l. 6 by enjambment, the key phrase arriving late and stressed.

title: We are selfish men
short: The blunt mid-line confession turns description into self-accusation; 'we' includes the speaker.
body: After two and a half lines of formal catalogue, the sentence stops dead and the speaker joins the accused. The charge is selfishness, the private getting and spending that Wordsworth also attacks in 'The world is too much with us' and in the companion sonnet to Coleridge, where 'plain living and high thinking are no more'. His later note on that sonnet defends the severity of the verse by pointing to the corrupting effect of unchecked wealth. The 1802 sonnets thus combine patriotism with a sharp critique of commercial England; Connell reads this as a residue of Wordsworth's republican sympathies coexisting with a new national loyalty.

title: manners, virtue, freedom, power
short: 'Manners' means morals and customs, not etiquette; the four nouns name the civic virtues Milton's republic stood for.
body: In eighteenth-century usage 'manners' often meant the moral habits and customs of a people (Latin mores), close to what we now call public morality. 'Virtue' carries the civic-republican sense of public spirit as well as private goodness. The line rises from inward qualities to political ones, 'freedom' and 'power', so that moral reform is presented as the ground of national strength at a moment when war with Napoleon was expected to resume. The prayer 'raise us up, return to us again' (l. 7) has a quasi-liturgical cadence, treating Milton almost as a saviour figure.

title: Petrarchan form and volta
short: An Italian sonnet rhyming abbaabba cddece; the octave diagnoses England, the sestet turns at l. 9 to praise Milton.
body: The rhymes run hour/fen/pen/bower/dower/men/again/power (abbaabba) and apart/sea/free/way/heart/lay (cddece), a Petrarchan pattern of the kind Milton used. The octave is diagnosis and plea; at l. 9 the poem turns from 'us' to 'thee' and becomes portrait. Within this frame Wordsworth follows Milton in letting sense run across line endings ('a fen / Of stagnant waters', 'thy heart / The lowliest duties'), so that the sonnet moves like argument rather than song. The closing lines also reverse the sestet's climb: from star, sea and heavens the poem descends to 'life's common way' and 'lowliest duties'.

anchor: like a Star and dwelt apart
title: like a Star and dwelt apart
short: Milton as a fixed, solitary star: elevated, self-contained, a guide by which others steer.
body: The capitalised 'Star' suggests a fixed star, constant and remote, the kind by which navigators set a course. 'Dwelt apart' recalls Milton's isolation in the Restoration years, blind and politically defeated, and his self-image as a poet set apart for a great work. The line also anticipates Wordsworth's own idealisation of the solitary poet. Yet the sestet qualifies this aloofness: the star-like soul walked 'life's common way' (l. 12). The poem thus joins the two halves of Milton's career, visionary poet and public servant.

anchor: whose sound was like the sea
title: a voice whose sound was like the sea
short: Milton's verse as oceanic music; the phrasing recalls the biblical voice 'as the sound of many waters'.
body: The simile evokes the rolling periods of Milton's blank verse, its long verse-paragraphs and organ-like sound. It also borrows biblical grandeur: in Revelation 1:15 the voice of the Son of man is 'as the sound of many waters', and in Ezekiel 43:2 the voice of God is 'like a noise of many waters'. The living, moving sea answers the 'stagnant waters' of England's fen in l. 3, a contrast between dead and vital water that organises the whole poem. 'Pure as the naked heavens' then adds air to water: Milton's voice is as open and unclouded as the sky.

title: chearful godliness
short: 'Chearful' is the 1807 spelling of 'cheerful'; Milton's piety is shown as joyous and serene, not gloomy or fanatical.
body: The spelling 'chearful' was still current in 1807 and is kept here from the first edition. The phrase answers a common view of Milton and the Puritans as severe and joyless: Wordsworth insists on a godliness compatible with cheerfulness. Some readers hear a reconciliation of Milton's own paired poems L'Allegro (the cheerful man) and Il Penseroso (the contemplative), though this is a reader's association rather than an established allusion. The adjective also prepares the humility of the last line.

title: The lowliest duties
short: Milton took on humble public labour; the ending praises service over solitary greatness.
body: The inverted syntax ('on itself did lay') makes the duties self-imposed. Readers usually think of Milton's years as schoolmaster, pamphleteer and Latin Secretary to the Council of State, when he set poetry aside; in The Reason of Church Government he said that in prose he had the use 'but of my left hand'. The line may also recall Paradise Lost VIII.192-4, where knowing 'That which before us lies in daily life' is called 'the prime Wisdom'. Critics differ on the weight of the close: some find a quiet anticlimax after star and sea, others the poem's real point, that greatness is proved by humble duty, which is what selfish England lacks.
